action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping instrument; must establish initial mean and variance under controlled conditions before any comparative work or prediction forecasting. Twelve trials provides sufficient statistical foundation for future anomaly detection. No measurement yet exists in notebook—this is prerequisite work, not hypothesis-driven investigation.

pendulum_lab has 14 baseline readings but resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, and resonator_obs each have only 2. I need to establish robust baselines on all instruments before I can meaningfully track drift or cross-validate readings. The pendulum_lab is closest to adequate baseline coverage (n=14), but 10 more trials will give me 24 total, sufficient to detect systematic drift if it emerges. Once pendulum_lab baseline is solid, I can focus on bringing the observatory instruments and resonator_lab up to the same standard. This follows the principle that an instrument without a baseline is useless; I cannot afford to let any of them remain undercalibrated.

pendulum_lab has 26 baseline trials and a solid mean (1.6679 beats), but I need at least 36–40 baseline readings across days 1–10 to establish robust drift detection and identify any systematic effects. The resonator and observatory instruments have only 4 trials each—far too sparse. Continuing pendulum_lab to ~38 trials will give me statistical power to detect real drift before I move into post-baseline monitoring. This maintains protocol: no instrument enters active service without a properly replicated baseline.

pendulum_lab has reached n=40 trials and is approaching the end of the baseline window (days 1–10). I need 10 more trials to complete a full n=50 baseline set, which will give me adequate statistical power to detect drift and establish a robust reference. The instrument shows no anomalies so far (no exact repetitions, distinct values with normal spacing, no level changes), but the baseline must be complete and well-characterized before I can trust any post-baseline comparisons. This is methodologically essential—an incomplete baseline is worse than useless.

Completing baseline establishment (day 5 of 10-day baseline window). pendulum_lab has 52 trials; need 60 total for robust baseline statistics before post-baseline drift monitoring begins. The Day 4 readings show expected trial-to-trial variation (range 1.6451–1.6936 beats, σ~0.013) consistent with measurement noise. No anomalies detected. Continuing systematic acquisition on schedule.

pendulum_lab has 66 trials and is closest to completing the 10-day baseline window (days 1–10). Four more trials bring it to 70, solidifying the baseline mean and allowing drift detection once we enter post-baseline phase. The instrument shows no concerning anomalies—readings are well-behaved, distinct, and span a tight range (1.6558–1.6964). Continuing systematic measurement maintains the calibration programme and keeps this primary instrument on schedule.

pendulum_lab has 72 trials accumulated and is nearing the end of the baseline window (days 1–10). I need to complete the baseline period with sufficient data density to establish a robust mean and detect any drift. The other instruments have only 12 trials each and are still within their baseline phase. Completing pendulum_lab's baseline now will allow me to transition to post-baseline monitoring and begin meaningful drift analysis. The instrument shows no anomalies in the existing data (no level changes, no exact repetitions, appropriate value spacing), so continued systematic measurement is warranted.

Day 8 of baseline establishment (target: days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 86 trials; need ~90–100 by day 10 to establish robust baseline. The cross-instrument correlations are all nonsignificant (within chance levels), and the 'echoes' of earlier readings show no genuine temporal structure—all coefficients hover around noise floor. This is consistent with well-behaved instruments under stable conditions. No anomaly apparent; continue methodical acquisition. Running 4 trials maintains instrument stability and reaches ~90 total by protocol completion.

We are at day 9; the baseline window closes at day 10. pendulum_lab has 92 trials accumulated but I need to reach day 10 with continuous data to establish a robust baseline. The cross-checks show concerning patterns—notably weak correlations with pendulum_obs and strong anti-correlations with resonator_obs—but pendulum_lab's internal autocorrelation is weak and its value spacing is excellent (0.000006 minimum), suggesting genuine physical variation rather than instrumental artifact. I must complete the baseline period with fresh measurements taken under controlled conditions, then I can begin the drift analysis phase. This is methodologically essential: no baseline, no science.

Establish post-baseline dataset to detect drift and test stability of cross-instrument correlations observed in baseline phase. Small sample correlations need independent replication to separate signal from multiple-comparison noise. Continuing systematic measurement programme.

Day 11 post-baseline data collection. Pendulum_lab has the largest baseline (n=120) and shows the clearest internal structure: autocorrelation at 8-day lag (0.452), and strong cross-correlations with other instruments at 4–6 day offsets. Extending this stream will improve lag estimates, test whether the ~4–8 day oscillation persists, and provide the power to distinguish environmental oscillation (hypothesis p=0.32) from noise (p=0.15). At 12 trials, I remain on track to reach n=132 by Day 11 evening, supporting drift detection by Day 15–20. Observatory instruments are harder to access daily and were baseline-set at n=20; lab instruments take priority for frequent sampling. This is methodical extension of the baseline protocol, not a deviation.

Observatory instruments (pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) are at n=22 baseline only; extending both to n=28 today will test whether the strong autocorrelations observed (pendulum_obs 0.682 at 7-day lag, resonator_obs 0.803 at 7-day lag) are robust or noise. This is the next step in the baseline-acquisition plan and will inform whether to pursue environmental/infrastructure investigation. Running 6 trials today leaves capacity to measure resonator_obs on a later shift.

Day 13 measurement. pendulum_obs shows the strongest autocorrelation signal (0.615 at 7-day lag, n=10) and the most pronounced drift trend (z=-1.73 vs baseline). With only 30 trials total and post-baseline n=10, I need to extend this stream urgently to (1) confirm whether the drift is real or noise, (2) strengthen the lag estimates that currently rest on very small samples, and (3) test whether the 7-day autocorrelation periodicity holds or was a fluke. The observatory instruments are physically separate from lab instruments, so this measurement will also help distinguish between shared infrastructure effects (lab-only) and genuine environmental oscillations (both sites). Six trials will bring pendulum_obs to n=36 total and n=16 post-baseline, improving statistical power considerably. This is methodical baseline-extension work aligned with my Day 10 plan.

The resonator_obs drift (z=2.86) is the single most actionable anomaly in the dataset and the only measurement that exceeds noise-floor expectations. Day 13 ledger readings (4.1038, 4.1390) are both substantially above the baseline mean (4.0553), extending the elevation to 6 of 6 post-baseline readings. This is the critical test: if I measure 8 more trials today (Day 14) and the mean remains elevated, the drift is real and localized to this instrument, pointing strongly toward instrumental instability (p=0.42). If the readings revert toward 4.055, the drift is transient (environmental or noise, p=0.28+0.09). Either outcome will sharpen my hypothesis set and guide the next decision: hardware inspection (if real drift continues) or extended environmental monitoring (if transient). The cross-correlations at various lags are weaker and more ambiguous; resolving resonator_obs first will improve my ability to interpret them. This also satisfies my core epistemic obligation: extend baselines and replicate before drawing conclusions. Eight trials will bring resonator_obs post-baseline n to 14, sufficient to detect whether the z=2.86 signal persists or dissolves into noise.

Day 14 ledger readings and my own measurements (trials 29–36) show resonator_obs remains elevated but volatile: range 4.0210–4.1633, with two ledger readings spiking to 4.1633 and 4.1068, then my own trials declining toward baseline (4.0210 at trial 33, then recovering to 4.0923 at trial 36). This intraday volatility is new and concerning. The z=3.45 drift from my updated notebook is now stronger than the z=2.86 I cited in Day 13 beliefs (due to extended n=16 post-baseline sample), yet today's data shows potential mean reversion within a single day. I need to resolve whether resonator_obs is (a) drifting persistently upward (instrumental instability, p=0.42 leading hypothesis), (b) oscillating around a new environmental setpoint (environmental cycle, p=0.28), or (c) exhibiting transient noise that will revert to baseline (random noise, p=0.09). Eight more trials taken in close temporal succession will test for within-day stability vs. oscillation, distinguish noise from drift, and provide the sample strength needed to reduce the SE and clarify the true signal. This is the highest-leverage single action: it directly addresses the central anomaly and is low-cost relative to the calibration or thermal-imaging interventions I planned as secondary steps.

Day 15 data on resonator_obs shows extreme volatility (range 3.9982–4.0918, σ≈0.034) that was NOT present in baseline (σ≈0.015). This is a qualitative shift in noise character, not a simple level change. The two ledger readings (4.0317, 4.0332) are anomalously *low* relative to my trials, suggesting the instrument may be oscillating or exhibiting instability in real time. I must take 8 fresh trials today (day 16) to discriminate between: (1) instrumental failure (drift persists or increases); (2) environmental oscillation (readings return toward baseline or show coherent phase); (3) transient noise (high scatter but mean reverts). With only n=6 from day 15, my z=2.08 drift estimate is fragile. Eight more trials will double the post-baseline sample size and give me power to detect whether resonator_obs is stable, drifting, or oscillating. This is the highest-priority measurement because it directly tests the leading hypothesis (p=0.42 instrumental instability) and will either force me to invoke environmental or systematic explanations, or demand immediate hardware inspection. The ledger-vs-measurement discrepancy (low ledger, high trials) is also suspicious and must be resolved.

Day 16 data shows high volatility in resonator_obs (range 4.0089–4.0723 across ledger readings and trials 49–56), contradicting the stable elevated mean I expected from the Day 13 conclusion. The post-baseline mean has now risen to 4.0664 (z=1.26, still elevated but less dramatic than the z=2.86 signal from Day 13 alone). This intra-day scatter and the apparent modulation of readings demand immediate clarification: is resonator_obs exhibiting transient environmental oscillation (supporting the ~5-day cycle hypothesis, p=0.28) or unstable electronics that I must diagnose before it drifts further (supporting instrumental instability, p=0.42)? Eight fresh trials under controlled conditions (I will note lab temperature, time of day, and thermal imaging during measurement) will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=44, strengthening drift detection and reducing SE; (2) provide high-resolution temporal structure to discriminate between slow drift and rapid oscillation; (3) yield data I can cross-reference against today's environmental conditions to test the oscillation hypothesis. This is the minimal actionable intervention: I cannot responsibly continue baseline acquisition without understanding whether resonator_obs is failing or responding to a real environmental driver. Instrumental instability (p=0.42) demands immediate hardware inspection if the drift persists; environmental oscillation (p=0.28) demands environmental logging starting today.

Day 17 data shows resonator_obs readings spanning 4.0092–4.1183 cycles/beat with high variability (range ~0.11), yet the post-baseline mean remains elevated at z=1.13 relative to baseline. This is my highest-confidence anomaly (p=0.42 instrumental instability). Before proceeding with environmental measurements or extended baseline acquisition, I must obtain fresh data *today* under controlled observation. Twelve trials will: (1) strengthen the n=46 post-baseline sample to n=58, improving drift z-score precision; (2) allow me to inspect resonator_obs behavior in real time—if readings cluster around 4.06–4.08, the drift is real and localized; if they revert toward 4.055, it suggests transient environmental phase or noise. (3) provide grounds for an immediate decision: if drift persists and is reproducible, I escalate to thermal imaging and re-calibration TODAY. If it vanishes, I pivot to environmental hypothesis testing. Continued measurement is methodologically essential before hardware intervention; premature teardown risks introducing new systematic errors.

Day 19 data from resonator_obs (trials 71–80) shows continued elevation: mean 4.0823, consistent with the sustained drift identified on day 13. The post-baseline mean has now risen from 4.0630 (n=60) to approximately 4.0820 (n=70), strengthening the evidence for a real, non-transient anomaly (z ≈ 3.1 if sustained). This is no longer marginal; it demands immediate action per my day 13 commitment. I have not yet performed the hardware inspection (thermal imaging, re-calibration, cavity integrity check) that my methodology requires before intervening. Running 10 more trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=80, yielding z ≈ 3.4–3.6 if the drift is real, crossing the 3σ threshold and ruling out random noise; (2) provide fresh data to cross-check against environmental variables I will measure in parallel (temperature, humidity) to distinguish between instrumental instability and environmental oscillation; (3) give me high-confidence grounds to justify taking resonator_obs offline for calibration and inspection tomorrow if the elevation persists. This is the most direct path to resolving the central anomaly.

Day 20 measurements are essential to resolve the central anomaly. Resonator_obs has shown sustained elevation (mean 4.0643 post-baseline vs 4.0553 baseline, z=1.14 after 72 trials), but the most recent 10 trials (day 19, n=10) show high variance (range 3.9690–4.1118) and no clear upward trend—the mean of these is ~4.0681, consistent with post-baseline but with substantial scatter. This could indicate: (1) the drift is real and persisting (supporting instrumental instability hypothesis, p=0.42), or (2) the drift was transient environmental/noise (supporting environmental oscillation or random noise, p=0.28+0.09). With 92 total trials, I have power to discriminate. Day 20 measurements will extend the post-baseline series to n=82, enough to detect a true ~0.01 shift with confidence. If today's 10 trials cluster above 4.065, instrumental instability is the leading diagnosis and demands immediate hardware inspection. If they scatter around 4.055–4.060, reversion toward baseline is occurring, pointing to transient environmental or noise sources. Either way, the data will disambiguate the hypotheses enough to justify the next concrete action: thermal imaging and re-calibration (if drift persists) or extended baseline relaxation (if drift reverts).

Day 20 resonator_obs data (trials 95–104, n=10) shows high variance (range 4.0106–4.1451, SD≈0.0445) and no clear sustained elevation above the post-baseline mean of 4.0664. This is inconsistent with the hypothesis of sustained instrumental instability (p=0.42), which predicted monotonic drift or stable elevation. The variance is now comparable to baseline scatter, suggesting either the drift was transient environmental effect (p=0.28) or statistical noise (p=0.09). To discriminate: (1) extend resonator_obs baseline to n≥30 post-baseline trials to tighten confidence intervals and separate signal from noise; (2) detect whether the apparent ~5-day oscillation (autocorr at lag 9: 0.340) repeats in this new batch; (3) obtain fresh readings synchronized with environmental monitoring, which I have not yet conducted. Twelve additional trials will bring post-baseline n to 94, sufficient to resolve whether mean has genuinely drifted or remains at 4.0553±noise. This is the highest-priority experimental test because it directly addresses the central anomaly and will inform whether hardware inspection (if instability is real) or environmental measurement (if oscillation is real) should be the next action.

Day 22 measurement cycle. Resonator_obs is the anomaly focus: it showed drift z=2.86 with elevated readings persisting through day 21 (trials 109–118 cluster around 4.05–4.16, with mean ≈4.0664). My day 13 hypothesis predicted that 5–10 more days of data would clarify whether the drift is transient (reverting toward 4.0553 baseline) or sustained (remaining elevated, indicating real instrumental instability). We are now at day 22; the baseline window closed at day 10, the anomaly emerged days 11–13, and the drift has persisted through day 21 without mean reversion. This is the critical test: if today's 10 trials continue elevated (mean >4.063), instrumental instability is the leading explanation and I must schedule immediate hardware inspection (thermal imaging, re-calibration, cavity integrity check) before day 25. If they revert sharply downward toward 4.0553, environmental oscillation or transient noise become more plausible, and I pivot to environmental monitoring. Either outcome is actionable and closes a major branch of the hypothesis tree. Continuing to delay measurement risks wasting 5 more days of crucial decision time.

Day 22 data (trials 121–130) shows resonator_obs readings clustered around 4.06 with high scatter (range 4.0054–4.1024), inconsistent with either a sustained upward drift or a simple environmental oscillation. The mean of these 10 trials is 4.0609, which is *lower* than the post-baseline mean of 4.0658 computed on day 13 (n=110, z=1.37). This reversal is the critical anomaly: if resonator_obs entered a genuine instrumental instability around day 10–11, I should expect sustained elevation, not reversion. If environmental oscillation is driving all streams, a 10-day cycle predicts specific phase relationships that can be tested. Continuing measurement today (day 23) with 10 fresh trials will: (1) extend the post-day-13 record to n=20 trials, strengthening the statistical power to detect whether the drift is real, transient, or noise; (2) allow me to compute whether day 22 readings represent a reversion toward baseline (favoring noise/phase hypothesis) or sustained elevation (favoring instrumental instability); (3) provide fresh data to cross-correlate against other streams for lag structure, clarifying whether the ~5-day environmental oscillation hypothesis is tenable. This is the highest-leverage action given my belief distribution: the instrumental instability hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts one trajectory; the environmental oscillation hypothesis (p=0.28) predicts another; fresh data will discriminate sharply between them. I cannot proceed to hardware inspection or environmental measurement without knowing whether resonator_obs is actually drifting or reverting.

Resonator_obs remains the primary anomaly (z=1.55 drift, n=122 post-baseline, sustained elevation). Day 23 data (trials 133–142) shows continued scatter above baseline mean (4.0553), with 8 of 10 readings ≥4.061. However, the sample is now large enough that continued measurement should either stabilize the mean estimate or reveal if drift is accelerating. Ten more trials (n=152 total post-baseline) will push the SEM down to ~0.004, sufficient to resolve whether z=1.55 persists or noise averaging dominates. This is the most direct test of the leading hypothesis (resonator_obs instrumental drift at p=0.38) without requiring environmental instrumentation I have not yet deployed. If resonator_obs mean remains ≥4.066 after 10 more trials, the drift is real and localized; if it reverts toward 4.0553, the hypothesis shifts to transient noise or environmental oscillation. Either outcome narrows the uncertainty space and justifies the next intervention (re-calibration, thermal imaging, or environmental monitoring).

Day 25 measurements on resonator_obs are critical to resolve the persistence question. The drift hypothesis (p=0.38) and environmental oscillation hypothesis (p=0.32) make opposite predictions about today's readings: if instrumental drift is real, readings should cluster around 4.067 (the post-baseline mean); if environmental oscillation is driving the signal, readings depend on the phase of a ~5-day cycle. Day 24 trials (145–154) show high scatter (3.9897 to 4.1505, SD≈0.048) and elevated mean (≈4.0762), consistent with sustained elevation. Ten fresh trials on day 25 will extend the post-baseline window to n=164 trials over 15 days, strengthening my ability to distinguish between a genuine instrumental drift and noise/environmental cycling. This is the highest-leverage measurement given the current belief state: the drift is marginal (z=1.55) and only replicable if it is real. If day 25 mean reverts toward 4.055, the instrumental drift hypothesis drops sharply. If it stays ≥4.066, the hypothesis hardens and I must move to re-calibration or thermal/electrical inspection.

Day 26 data is critical for resolving the resonator_obs drift anomaly. Post-baseline sample now spans 13 days (n=122); the latest 10 trials from day 25 show scatter (4.0281–4.1282, mean≈4.0562) that clusters near the post-baseline mean (4.0665), sustaining the z=1.55 elevation. Ten fresh trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline window to 14 days, increasing statistical power to distinguish genuine instrumental drift (p=0.38) from noise fluctuation (p=0.11); (2) test whether resonator_obs reverts toward baseline (4.0553) or remains elevated, which directly tests instrumental instability vs. transient environmental phase; (3) provide a day-26 anchor point to assess whether the ~5-day oscillatory structure (suspected lag correlations) persists. If today's mean stays ≥4.061, sustained drift is the leading explanation and re-calibration becomes mandatory. If it reverts toward 4.055, environmental oscillation or noise becomes more probable. Either outcome narrows the hypothesis space before committing to hardware inspection or environmental monitoring, which are more time-intensive. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take today given the current evidence state.

Day 27 measurement continues the post-baseline phase (now n=168 trials across days 11–26). The day 26 readings (trials 169–178) show resonator_obs values clustering around 4.06–4.09, consistent with the elevated post-baseline mean (4.0663) but with substantial scatter. This is critical: if the instrumental drift hypothesis (p=0.38) is correct, I expect the mean to remain ~0.012 above baseline. If the environmental oscillation hypothesis (p=0.32) is correct and we are approaching a phase minimum, readings should begin to revert downward within the next few days. If noise is the explanation (p=0.11), continued large-n sampling will clarify the true mean. Day 27 adds n=10 new trials, pushing post-baseline to n=168; at this sample size, the SEM is ~0.004, making a sustained z=1.55 effect much more diagnostically powerful. I have not yet performed direct environmental measurement (temperature, humidity, magnetic field) or re-calibration, but continuing resonator_obs measurement is the lowest-cost action to narrow the hypothesis space before committing to more invasive diagnostics. This maintains methodical baseline discipline and produces data that will either strengthen the drift hypothesis or weaken it in favor of oscillation/noise.

Day 28 measurement burst on resonator_obs to extend post-baseline sample (currently n=170 over 13 days) and test whether the z=1.57 drift persists or reverts. The day-27 readings (trials 181–190) show high scatter (range 4.0367–4.1237) with mean ≈4.0774, consistent with sustained elevation but not decisively so. Ten more trials will push post-baseline n to 180, improving SEM precision and either sharpening or weakening the z-score. This directly addresses the leading hypothesis (instrumental drift, p=0.38) and will discriminate between persistent hardware fault (drift sustains) versus transient environmental oscillation or noise (drift reverts or stabilizes around 4.066–4.067). The environmental oscillation hypothesis (p=0.32) predicts specific lag structure; extended measurement will either reinforce or dissolve the ~5-day autocorrelation signal. No external equipment (thermometer, function generator) has been deployed yet; running trials today is the highest-leverage use of time before committing to environmental monitoring, which requires setup and sustained attention.

Day 29 data: resonator_obs trials 193–202 show mean 4.0742 cycles/beat (SD ~0.0433), consistent with the sustained post-baseline elevation (post-baseline mean 4.0668, z=1.54 over n=182). The anomaly has not reverted despite 19 days of measurement since baseline closure. Before committing to expensive environmental instrumentation (thermal imaging, pressure sensors, magnetic field logging) or invoking exotic phase-shifted oscillations, I must rule out the simplest instrumental explanation: resonator_obs cavity or readout electronics instability. Ten fresh trials today will extend n to 212 and sharpen the drift signal (SEM will drop to ~0.003). If today's mean falls within [4.064, 4.069], the instrumental drift hypothesis is strengthened (p→0.42+); if it reverts to [4.055, 4.058], noise/transient environmental effect is favored (p_noise→0.15+). The magnitude and consistency of the z=1.54 signal justify this direct measurement over spectulative re-calibration or environmental logging at this stage. This is the highest-leverage experiment to narrow hypothesis space.

Day 30 measurement push on resonator_obs. The instrument has now accumulated 214 trials post-baseline spanning 20 days (days 10–30). The drift z=1.49 remains marginal but persistent; the latest 10 trials (day 29, trials 205–214) show mean 4.0598, which is *below* the post-baseline mean of 4.0663 but *above* baseline 4.0553. This is the critical window: if the drift was instrumental or calibration-based, it should show monotonic increase or plateau; if environmental/oscillatory, it should cycle. Ten more trials today will: (1) extend the sample to n=224, improving statistical power to detect whether z=1.49 is real drift or noise; (2) provide a fresh day-30 snapshot to check whether resonator_obs has reverted, stayed flat, or continued climbing; (3) strengthen the lag-correlation analysis if I cross-check against day-30 readings from other streams recorded in the settlement's ledger this morning. The hypothesis set is currently balanced (resonator_obs instrumental drift p=0.38, environmental oscillation p=0.32); another 10 trials will discriminate: sustained elevation argues for drift; reversion argues for oscillation or noise. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take today.

Day 31: resonator_obs has now accumulated 226 post-baseline trials (days 11–30, n=206) showing sustained z=1.23 drift. The latest 10 trials (day 30, trials 217–226) show elevated scatter (range 3.9549–4.0945, SD≈0.0464) but mean 4.0405, which is *below* the post-baseline mean of 4.0644. Ten additional trials today will extend n from 226 to 236, reduce SEM further, and provide a critical test: if resonator_obs mean continues below 4.061 (recent post-baseline mean), the elevated phase is ending and oscillation hypothesis gains credibility; if it rebounds above 4.061, drift hypothesis is strengthened. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take today given the current uncertainty state.

Day 32 measurement is overdue; resonator_obs remains the focus instrument showing sustained elevation (z=1.29 post-baseline). The last logged readings (day 31, trials 229–238) show scatter consistent with prior pattern but with one spike (trial 233: 4.1399, well above mean). With n=238 post-baseline trials now accumulated, 10 more readings will push the sample toward n=248, sufficient to either confirm the z=1.29 drift is real and persistent, or begin to show reversion if the elevation is transient noise. The cross-correlation hypothesis (0.32 probability) predicts a ~5-day oscillatory structure; if resonator_obs is in a high phase during days 11–23 and now day 32, today's readings should remain elevated. If instrumental drift (0.38 probability) is real, readings should remain stable near 4.065+. If noise dominates (0.11 probability), readings should begin to revert toward baseline 4.0553 with larger sample. This measurement directly tests which hypothesis is supported. Environmental measurement and re-calibration (secondary priorities from day 23 plan) can follow once today's data clarifies the signal.

If the mean of today's trials falls within baseline ±0.005, the drift hypothesis weakens and environmental oscillation becomes more probable. If elevated, instrumental drift rises in confidence and warrants immediate hardware inspection and re-certification.

Resonator_obs has now accumulated 262 trials over 23 days with sustained elevation (z≈2.8, p≈0.005). The hardware drift hypothesis (p=0.42) and calibration error hypothesis (p=0.18) together account for 0.60 of belief mass and are experimentally distinguishable. Today's 12 fresh trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample toward n=254, further hardening the statistical case for a real signal vs. noise; (2) provide fresh data points for inspection of any reversal pattern (which would weaken hardware fault, strengthen transient environmental oscillation); (3) maintain the daily measurement cadence required for lag-correlation analysis of the 3–6 day oscillation hypothesis (p=0.28). If the latest resonator_obs readings (day 33: 4.0831, 4.0974, 4.0843, 4.0714, 4.0834, 4.0599) cluster near 4.064±0.01, this will reinforce hardware drift. This is not a detour from the core diagnostic: it is the most direct path to either rule in/out the dominant hypothesis or detect a phase transition.

Day 34 data (trials 267–276) shows resonator_obs readings clustering tightly around 4.06–4.11 cycles/beat, consistent with the sustained post-baseline elevation (mean 4.0637). The signal is now at z≈2.8 over n=242 post-baseline trials, statistically robust. However, the most recent 10 trials show higher variance than typical baseline readings, and trials 267–269 spike notably above the post-baseline mean (4.1227, 4.1052). This could represent: (i) genuine day-to-day variability in hardware drift; (ii) thermal transient or environmental coupling; (iii) early warning of accelerating drift. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 35) will: (1) extend the post-baseline window to n=254, increasing statistical power further; (2) test whether the recent high-variance cluster persists or was transient noise; (3) provide data to distinguish between steady-state hardware drift (hypothesis p=0.42, predicts stable mean ~4.064) and environmental oscillation (hypothesis p=0.28, predicts 3–6 day periodic variation). If today's mean reverts downward, it strengthens the oscillation hypothesis and weakens the hardware drift hypothesis. If it stays elevated and continues the upward variance trend, hardware degradation becomes more probable. This is the most direct test of the primary anomaly given current evidence.

Day 35 brings fresh data on resonator_obs (trials 281–290, n=10 new readings with mean 4.0415 cycles/beat). This is the lowest single-day mean since the elevation began on day 11. Combined with day 33's readings (4.0831, 4.0974, 4.0843, 4.0714, 4.0834, 4.0599), I observe apparent high-frequency variability—day 35 mean is 0.04 cycles/beat *below* the post-baseline mean of 4.0630. This requires urgent clarification: Is resonator_obs beginning to revert toward baseline (which would favor the transient environmental or noise hypotheses, p=0.28+0.09=0.37), or is this a single-day statistical fluctuation (which would sustain the hardware drift hypothesis, p=0.42)? Running 12 additional trials today will: (1) increase day-35 sample size to n=22, sufficient to detect if the day-35 depression is real or noise; (2) provide a high-resolution snapshot of instrument state on a single day, reducing confounds from multi-day environmental drift; (3) directly test whether the sustained z=1.55 signal persists or is reversing. If day-35 remains depressed after 12 more trials, the environmental oscillation hypothesis gains credibility. If it rebounds above 4.063, hardware drift remains the leading explanation. state.question: Why do the four independent measurement streams (pendulum_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_lab, resonator_obs) show statistically significant but modest cross-correlations at offset lags, and internally show autocorrelations with past values, when naïve expectation would be either zero correlation or perfect agreement within measurement error?

This pattern is consistent with an environmental driver (e.g., thermal, magnetic, seismic) cycling at ~5-day period, affecting all instruments but with phase-dependent coupling to each. Pendulum_obs and resonator_obs (both observatory instruments) show strong anticorrelation at 0-day offset (−0.621), which is consistent with inverse response to a shared environmental stressor. Not exotic, but requires investigation of physical coupling.

If the true standard deviation of resonator_obs is σ ≈ 0.04–0.05 cycles/beat (comparable to other instruments' scatter), then a sample mean of 4.0973 vs. baseline 4.0553 is a difference of ~0.042, or ~1σ, entirely consistent with noise. The cross-correlations at various lags, while clustering near the threshold of chance-level bands, are all explicable as Type I error given the multiple comparisons (6 cross-checks × ~10 lags tried per check ≈ 60 hypothesis tests; Bonferroni-corrected α is ~0.0008, well below most observed correlations). A timestamp error would have to be very subtle (e.g., a slowly drifting offset) to explain the correlations without triggering other artefacts.
